title: What are Flink's three time semantics (event time = when it happened, processing time = system clock, ingestion time = when it entered the pipeline) and when do you use each?
shortTitle: What are Flink's three time semantics

s1_definition.profdef: Flink supports three notions of time. Event time is the timestamp embedded in each record describing when the event actually occurred at its source. Processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the moment it handles the record. Ingestion time is the timestamp assigned by the Flink source operator when the record first enters the pipeline. Event time gives deterministic, replayable, out-of-order-tolerant results through watermarks, processing time gives the lowest latency but non-deterministic results, and ingestion time is a middle ground that is stable but ignores true source delays.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh swipes his card at an ATM at exactly 10:00:00. Event time is the clock printed on the receipt at the ATM, the true moment it happened. Ingestion time is the time stamped by the National Bank of India's front-gate security the moment the transaction message walks through the bank's door. Processing time is whatever time the back-office clerk's wall clock shows when the clerk finally gets around to processing the slip. If the network was slow, all three can differ by minutes. Event time tells the truth about when it happened, ingestion time tells when it reached us, and processing time tells when we touched it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Event time is when it happened, ingestion time is when it entered Flink, and processing time is when the operator handled it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flink supports three notions of time. Event time is the timestamp embedded in each record describing when the event actually occurred at its source. Processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the moment it handles the record. Ingestion time is the timestamp assigned by the Flink source operator when the record first enters the pipeline. Event time gives deterministic, replayable, out-of-order-tolerant results through watermarks, processing time gives the lowest latency but non-deterministic results, and ingestion time is a middle ground that is stable but ignores true source delays.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh swipes his card at an ATM at exactly 10:00:00. Event time is the clock printed on the receipt at the ATM, the true moment it happened. Ingestion time is the time stamped by the National Bank of India's front-gate security the moment the transaction message walks through the bank's door. Processing time is whatever time the back-office clerk's wall clock shows when the clerk finally gets around to processing the slip. If the network was slow, all three can differ by minutes. Event time tells the truth about when it happened, ingestion time tells when it reached us, and processing time tells when we touched it.

**One line to remember:** Event time is when it happened, ingestion time is when it entered Flink, and processing time is when the operator handled it.

sections.s2_technical:
Event time is the timestamp carried inside the event itself, for example the point-of-sale time embedded in a transaction. You tell Flink how to extract it with a timestamp assigner inside a watermark strategy: `WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).withTimestampAssigner((event, ts) -> event.getPosTimeMillis())`. Event time is the gold standard because results are deterministic and replayable. If you reprocess the same data a week later, event-time windows produce exactly the same answer, because the grouping depends on the data, not on when you run the job. The cost is latency and complexity: you need watermarks to decide when a window is complete, and you must decide how long to wait for stragglers.

Processing time uses the operator machine's system clock. A processing-time window of one minute simply groups whatever records arrive in the next sixty seconds of wall-clock time. It needs no watermarks and no timestamps, so it has the lowest latency and the simplest setup. The downside is that it is non-deterministic: the same records replayed at a different speed, or after a failure and recovery, land in different windows, and network hiccups distort the results. You use processing time when you only care about throughput-style metrics where approximate grouping is fine, like a rough per-minute dashboard that nobody audits.

Ingestion time assigns the timestamp at the source operator when the record enters Flink, then behaves like event time downstream, with automatic watermarks. It is more stable than processing time because all downstream operators agree on one timestamp, but it still ignores the true delay between when the event happened and when it reached Flink, so a transaction delayed by a slow mobile network is still bucketed by arrival, not by occurrence. In modern Flink you rarely pick ingestion time explicitly; you either use event time for correctness or processing time for simplicity. The senior nuance is that event time is almost always the right default for financial and audit workloads, because regulators and reconciliation care about when money moved, not when a server happened to process the message.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs an end-of-day settlement report that counts how much each account transacted in each one-minute slot. The ATMs and point-of-sale terminals stamp each transaction with the true time it happened. During peak hours the message queue backs up, so some transactions reach the settlement job minutes after they occurred. If the report grouped by the clerk's processing clock, a transaction that truly happened at 09:59:59 but was processed at 10:03 would be counted in the wrong business minute, and the next day's reconciliation against the card network would not match. This is exactly why event time is required: the report must group by when the money actually moved.

Problem 2 — A separate operations dashboard just wants a live "transactions handled per minute by our servers" health metric, where nobody audits the exact grouping and the only goal is to see throughput in real time with the lowest possible lag. For that, processing time is perfect because it is simple, needs no watermarks, and reflects what the servers are doing right now. This contrast is exactly the tradeoff: event time for the auditable settlement report, processing time for the throughput health dashboard.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that processes the same transactions under all three time semantics so you can see the different buckets. We create a `TransactionEvent` with a true event time, and we simulate an ingestion time and a processing time that differ because of a delay. A `TimeSemanticsBucketer` assigns each event to a one-minute window three ways: by event time, by ingestion time, and by processing time. A `SettlementReporter` uses the event-time buckets for the auditable report, and a `ThroughputMonitor` uses processing-time buckets for the live health metric. A `TimeSemanticsDemo` main class feeds a delayed transaction and prints how the three semantics place it in different minutes, proving why the choice matters.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transaction for Rajesh (SAV2001) of 5000 rupees that truly happened at 09:59:59 (event time 59 seconds in our timeline), entered Flink at 10:00:30 (ingestion time 90 seconds), and was processed at 10:03:00 (processing time 240 seconds), with a one-minute window.

Step 1: The settlement reporter receives the event and buckets it by event time. The event time 59 seconds floors to minute zero, which is the 09:59 business slot. The 5000 rupees is correctly added to the 09:59 total, matching when the money actually moved.

Step 2: For comparison, the bucketer computes the ingestion-time bucket. The ingestion time 90 seconds floors to minute 60000, the 10:00 slot. So if we had used ingestion time, this transaction would be counted one minute late, in 10:00 instead of 09:59.

Step 3: The throughput monitor buckets the same event by processing time. The processing time 240 seconds floors to minute 240000, the 10:03 slot. For the live health dashboard this is exactly right: our servers handled this message at 10:03, so the throughput metric for 10:03 increments.

Step 4: The contrast is now visible. The same single transaction is in three different minutes depending on the semantic. For the auditable settlement report, only event time is correct, because reconciliation with the card network is based on when the swipe happened. For the operational throughput dashboard, processing time is correct, because it measures server activity.

Step 5: The demo prints all three buckets side by side so the reader sees the gap. In production, the settlement job would attach a watermark strategy with an event-time assigner, while the throughput job would use a processing-time window with no watermark at all.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] SETTLEMENT (event-time) SAV2001 amount 5000.00 -> minute 0
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] THROUGHPUT (processing-time) handled 1 txn -> minute 240000
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Event-time bucket    = 0
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Ingestion-time bucket= 60000
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Processing-time bucket= 240000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink gives you three ways to reason about time, and picking the right one is one of the most important decisions in a streaming job. Event time is the timestamp carried inside the record itself, describing when the event actually happened at its source, such as the moment a card was swiped. Processing time is the wall-clock time of the machine running the operator at the instant it handles the record. Ingestion time is the timestamp the source operator stamps the moment the record first enters Flink, which then behaves like event time downstream. Event time is deterministic and replayable because the grouping depends only on the data, so reprocessing the same stream later gives identical results, but it needs watermarks to decide when a window is complete. Processing time has the lowest latency and needs no watermarks, but it is non-deterministic, because the same records replayed at a different speed or after a recovery land in different windows. Ingestion time sits in between: it is stable across operators but still ignores the true delay between occurrence and arrival.

The rule I follow is simple. If the result must be correct, auditable, or replayable, I use event time, because the business cares about when the thing actually happened, not when a server got around to it. If I only need a rough, low-latency operational metric and nobody will audit the exact grouping, I use processing time because it is simpler and faster. Ingestion time is rarely the explicit choice today, because in practice you either want event-time correctness or processing-time simplicity.

At the National Bank of India this distinction was concrete. Our end-of-day settlement report absolutely had to use event time, because it is reconciled against the card network by the business minute when money moved, and during peak hours the queue backed up so processing time would have placed transactions in the wrong minute and broken reconciliation. We attached a watermark strategy with a timestamp assigner that read the point-of-sale time. In parallel, our operations health dashboard used processing-time windows with no watermarks, because it only answered "how many transactions are our servers handling right now," and simplicity and low latency mattered more than source-true grouping. Being able to explain why the same transaction lands in a different minute under each semantic, and why event time is non-negotiable for anything auditable, is exactly what separates someone who has run Flink in production from someone who has only read the docs.
